FSEC (Faculty Senate Executive Committee) Meeting Minutes Date: Wednesday, October 15, 2025 - Time: 10:00 AM – 12:00 noon Pastore Hall, Room 224 - Remote option via ZOOM Action Items: Staff will follow up with AVP Lavan about sharing the Academic Program Review Handbook/Manual that his office is developing.
FSEC awaits reviews by CBUM regarding proposed legislation and comments from TAAC regarding required syllabus statements.
Liaisons are asked to monitor progress and ensure written responses are provided.
Sen.
Trimm will provide the draft statement on campus police as relates to ICE to the SCLC so they might make recommendations.
Staff will invite the VP RED to an FSEC meeting soon to discuss “required training mandates” and myriad other research-related interests.
Sen.
Trimm will continue fact-finding related to policies that would apply to recording classroom activities and otherwise preventing disruptive behavior (politically motivated or otherwise) in the classroom. 1.
Call to Order - FS President Williams called the meeting to order at 10:01.
VP Preisser and Sens.
Daniels, Trimm and Van Wyk were present, along with ex officio member Ted Walls. 2.

Minutes for approval - Minutes of the 10/8/25 meeting.
The minutes were approved as edited. 3.
Guests: Christopher Lavan, Assoc.
Vice Provost for Advancement of Teaching and Learning, and Assoc.
Professor of Education Shane Tutwiler, Chair, Joint Committee for Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment (JAPROA) joined the meeting.
AVP Lavan started off by outlining the work of the ATL office, noting that it supports the work of committees like JAPROA and JCODL in an advisory and consultative way.
Some history and background was provided on the work of prior iterations of these committees and by former key staffers in the ATL office.
AVP Lavan and Chair Tutwiler stressed that the faculty-led committees retain the authority to conduct reviews within well-established processes, but the scope of that authority seems to confuse some faculty members.
It was noted that JAPROA is a newer committee that only experienced its first full operational year in AY24-25.

Committee members too struggled with the line between “advising” and “approving.” In short, when an undergraduate program is proposed by a department or college, the outcomes assessment portion of that proposal is assigned to JAPROA, which undertakes its work with assistance from the ATL office.
Also, the office has been developing a “Manual” or handbook that outlines the academic program review process which should become a valuable resource for departments undergoing reviews.
Chair Tutwiler noted that the guidance is drawn from Chapter 8 of the University Manual and the committee is keenly interested in simplifying the process to make it easier for departments to undertake.
He considers the work of his committee to be invaluable in guiding metaprocesses and ensuring that the university, through all aggregated academic units, continues to learn from self-study and reflection, and therefore improves and succeeds.
While JAPROA’s role involves providing feedback on outcomes assessments, they can only adopt and forward recommendations, but the final decisions always rest in the departments.

Wrapping up, FSEC members suggested that the draft manual be shared with the membership, and the committees might consider a graphic presentation of their workflows and processes which might enhance understanding. 4.
Priority Items 4.1 Green Hall Meeting Prep (10/29) - Several potential agenda items were discussed for the joint meeting between the FSEC and the university President, Provost and Vice Provost.
These ranged from the Federal Department of Education’s higher education “Compact,” to 1

department-level system administrator permissions from IT services.
The final list of talking points will be determined next week. 4.2 Meeting Prep October 16 Senate meeting - The Committee revisited the initiatives being formally introduced this month and discussed presentations.
There are some unknowns in that it is difficult to predict how long some presentations will run.
Standing committee chairs have been asked to be brief and it is hoped the annual photograph can be accomplished expeditiously. 4.3 Set weekly meeting schedule for spring semester - As not everyone continues to be available on Wednesday mornings next semester, staff will administer an availability poll asap. 5.
Continued Items 5.1 Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - Two newly submitted concerns were addressed, one of which was a reiteration of previous submission. 5.2 Committee Assignment Updates - Finalize Joint Committees - Several candidates have been contacted and responses should be forthcoming.
Most open seats are ready for appointments on 10/16. 5.3 Elimination of Budget Statement Requirement - Tabled to next week. 5.4 Graduate School external report - Pres.

Williams has mentioned the report to the Vice Provost in hopes of learning more about the administration’s reaction to it.
The Full FSEC will plan to discuss the content at their joint 10/29 meeting with administrators. 5.5 Centers and Institutes Discussion - continued discussion, esp. revisions to UM Sec. 8.90.20 - The CIRC has the draft proposal and is reviewing it.
Pres.
Williams is meeting with the Provost and Vice Provost about the specific proposal on 10/24. 6.
Updates 6.1 Updates (meetings with administrators, other committee meetings) i.
APC Meeting 10/14/25 - Pres.
Williams explained that he had voted against the tuition policy as presented, but approval was granted by the APC and it will now go to the BOT for adoption.
Current BOT members, relative to governance under the Board of Education, while having espoused a commitment to accessibility, seem distanced from RI voters and taxpayers in a way that might put them out of touch with the average student and their demographics and means.
Other positions expressed by Pres.

Williams included concerns about the role of market forces in determining tuition, fees, and charges and the real versus perceived transparency of approval procedures for changes to tuition, fees, and charges.
All members of APC were willing to have the deep conversations necessary to effect a comprehensive reorientation of the tuition policy, but everyone, including Pres.
Williams, recognized that there was insufficient time available for such conversations to affect the current draft language, which needs to be approved before the end of the calendar year, and that the mooted policy was better than no policy at all.
It is unknown as yet if the student and faculty representatives to the BOT will make comments during the review and adoption process.
Pres.
Williams will reach out to the faculty representative in advance of the vote.
It was noted that faculty members, and especially the FS President, could speak on this topic during public comment at the BOT meeting if so desired.
While most policies are on a five-year review cycle, APC members expressed a willingness to circle back to this one much sooner than that. ii.

Other - The administration has completed a draft of its UM Chp. 2 updates.
It will be transmitted to FSEC and CBUM soon for comment.
The FS President has also touched base with the Vice Provost about the development of training for faculty members regarding FOIA/APRA responsibilities.
Updates will be forthcoming.
The administration is anxious to implement cross-enrollment of 7- and 2

14-week course offerings.Myriad logistical, philosophical, and financial issues must be discussed and sorted before this occurs..
These range from logistical and operational roadblocks related to billing and financial aid, to bigger picture academic questions like how students will manage the unique workloads associated with simultaneous enrollment in both programs, and how departments and colleges will manage budgets when significant resources stand to be diverted away from them in favor of Online Programs.
Circling back to an issue raised at last week’s FSEC, the SCLC will be asked to look at the draft policy related to campus police and an ICE presence on campus.
The Committee should review the draft and comment and also make suggestions regarding the appropriate means and timeline for getting the policy in front of the PSAC and/or other appropriate groups/administrators.

FSEC will also bring this up in their meeting with VP Benson on 10/22. 6.2 Reviving work of restructured JCODL - a meeting is set for tomorrow with the Vice Provost and ATL, URI Online, and OSI representatives in hopes of advancing a draft proposal. 6.3 NECHE Accreditation - A libraries-related letter of concern has been submitted.
The deadline has been extended until 10/20. 6.4 Required Syllabus Statements - assigned to TAAC.
FSEC awaits their review. 6.5 University Diversity Council.
Pres.
Williams reported on comments made at PSC and outlined topics for further discussion with relevant administrators. 7.
Report of the Coordinator – none. 8.
New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda.
Civil rights "training" and other Federal, state, and other training mandates - The concern is that these requirements add-up for faculty and in some cases, have become burdensome.
Ideas for consolidating the trainings or otherwise reducing this burden were solicited.
It was noted that when funding agencies impose these requirements, they are simply not optional and compliance is compulsory.

In other cases, like “in-house” cyber-security training, for example, faculty time constraints and the need for efficiency need to be understood and respected.
It was suggested that this conversation needs to be moved up the administrative chain as the FS cannot pursue a solution unilaterally.
As a starting place, an invitation will be sent to VP RED Jenkins to join the FSEC for a conversation about this and other matters.
Separately, a concern was expressed about the possible need for a policy that might prevent recording and other disruptive intrusions into classroom activity for political purposes.
It was noted there are already rules in place regarding recording (FERPA) and faculty are encouraged to reinforce the prohibitions (barring pre-established exceptions/accommodations) in the classroom, and via the syllabus and other outreach.
There may be other policies - related to harassment and endangering behavior, for example, that might also be relevant.
It seems to make sense to consolidate all related policies in one place as a convenient and useful resource for faculty and students.
Sen Trimm will further explore this issue. 9.

Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting. 10.
Adjournment - the meeting adjourned at 12:02 pm. 3

FSEC (Faculty Senate Executive Committee) Meeting Minutes Date: Wednesday, October 22, 2025 - Time: 10:00 AM – 12:00 noon Pastore Hall, Room 224 - Remote option via ZOOM Action Items: FSEC members should feel free to add topics for discussion before the 10/29 meeting in Green Hall.

Guests at 11:15 AM: Dan Moos, Chief of Staff to Vice President for Administration and Finance Benson, and Karl Calvo - AVP Facilities.

AVP Calvo offered a slide presentation explaining how his office is structured into divisions dealing with long range planning and design, current operations, small projects, and large-scale construction.
Major projects planned include construction of additional undergraduate dorms, on-going improvements at the Bay Campus, and a new bio-medical sciences building, among others.
Of particular interest to FSEC were the future of the University Library and the need for additional graduate- and international-student housing.
Other issues the conversation touched upon included parking, lighting and other infrastructure improvements (like water treatment facilities and re-paving).
Google Maps layers of the university’s geographic information system were briefly discussed and it was noted that better mapping and better messaging about maps available would help address needs like understanding ease of access for members of the disabilities community and things like gender neutral restroom availability.
Classroom issues were also discussed, especially appropriateness of available spaces in relation to teaching style.

This process is complex and involves Dean-level requests for fit-outs of specific spaces, but also typically involves the JCSC, building managers, IT Services and CMS.
While the process may or may not have been well-coordinated in the past, AVP Calvo encouraged concerned faculty to reach out with specific concerts about their instructional spaces going forward.
Questions were asked about the wrap-up of the consultative process which led to the recently adopted Campus Master Plan, and whether all members of consultative committees had an opportunity to express their opinions of the draft plan.
Specifically, a final meeting of the committee was never convened and it is not clear whether originally planned broader ‘testing’ of the plan with campus groups as outlined by Sasaki happened.
It was conceded that given the outside consultants involved in the project, coordination may not have been as robust as it could have been and AVP Calvo offered to inquire about why the final meeting was not convened..
The conversation ended with a discussion of the library.
It was noted that faculty have grave concerns about the library’s current condition and its future.

AVP Calvo explained that the library’s location has been problematic from the start in that it was built over a stream and this has created ongoing issues with moisture in the building.
Several small projects are planned in the near term (HVAC, air handlers, roof - to deal with features/equipment that have reached the end of their useful life), but the university is also planning a $45 million renovation which will be a longer term project, perhaps in conjunction with the state archives. 1

Now that the university has sunset its administrative committee responsible for providing guidance and advice during the transition, it is unclear what how the BAC should focus its efforts.
It has no administrative counterpart and no clear nexus of cooperation with key administrators.

Past President Walls noted that models from peer institutions were used in developing the legislation that created the BAC.
Faculty-forward institutions like Tufts have a long history of having a permanent, standing committee responsible for weighing in on budget matters.
Given that implementation details of the new budget model remain unavailable, it was agreed that new processes and procedures still hold the potential to negatively impact faculty (through program consolidations and other potential outcomes).

It was noted that a retired faculty member for many years tracked revenues by source, especially state support for the university, and university expenditures.
Continuation of such tracking might be a worthwhile task for a committee of faculty.
The Committee also serves to act as a second set of eyes on decision making and is a formal body that can hear faculty concerns and advocate on their behalf.
